notes: Slice 'letalone', 1879-1969: from Cooley's 'right to be let alone' and the Kodak through the first privacy statute, the census/registration abuses of the 1930s-40s, post-war human-rights law and the 1960s databank fight, to Katz, Title III and Germany's 1969 Mikrozensus decision. Method: every quote was captured with tools/fetch-text.py and checked with --check (FOUND) against the URL given; PDFs are OCR text layers, so quotes keep OCR quirks (e.g. Cooley's 'immunity : to', hearing hyphens such as 'commit- tee') and line-break hyphens are removed as the checker does. Blocked sites and workarounds: HathiTrust (Cloudflare) blocked the 1879 first edition of Cooley, so the 1888 2nd edition (the one Warren and Brandeis cite) is quoted and the 1879 date rests on the HathiTrust catalogue plus the preface dated Dec. 1878; nysenate.gov, metmuseum.org, BrooklynWorks and lawcat.berkeley.edu were read through Wayback Machine snapshots; coe.int treaty pages and pace.coe.int (403) were not readable, so the ECHR entry-into-force date (3 Sept 1953) and PACE Recommendation 509 (1968) are omitted; ssa.gov (403) blocked the Social Security number history, so no SSN event. Not verified / gaps: Seltzer 1998 (Population and Development Review 24:3) and Seltzer & Anderson's 2007 PAA paper were not read directly - the Dutch register rests on Seltzer & Anderson 2001 (Social Research), read from a course-reader copy (JSTOR 40971467 is the canonical, paywalled record); the Japanese-American microdata finding rests on Scientific American's 2007 report of that paper plus Ruggles & Magnuson 2023; the Kaysen task-force report (1966), Arthur Miller's 1967 Atlantic article and Barron's 1979 Suffolk article were not read (only cited via other sources); Westin's Privacy and Freedom (1967) was not read - his p. 7 definition is quoted from Margulis (J. Social Issues 2003); the Pavesich opinion is read on vLex (syllabus and opening only); the Roberson copy is an excerpt hosted by Hofstra. Venue details not in the cited texts (Palais de Chaillot, Palazzo Barberini, Supreme Court in the Old Senate Chamber, BVerfG building) are flagged in locationNote. Edwin Black's IBM and the Holocaust was not read; the IBM myth record relies on USHMM. All sources are CONFIRMED (fetched and quote FOUND); none PENDING.

events.title: Judge Cooley calls personal immunity a right “to be let alone”
events.place: University of Michigan Law Department, Ann Arbor, Michigan (published by Callaghan & Company, Chicago)
events.summary: Judge Thomas M. Cooley of the University of Michigan published A Treatise on the Law of Torts with Callaghan & Company of Chicago; his preface is dated Ann Arbor, December 1878 and the first edition bears the date 1879. In a passage on assault he wrote that “the right to one's person may be said to be a right of complete immunity: to be let alone.” The phrase sits on page 29 of the second edition (1888), the page Warren and Brandeis cited in 1890.
events.significance: The phrase that became privacy's slogan began as a description of freedom from physical assault — privacy as a wall around the body — not as control over information.

sources.institution: Callaghan & Company, Chicago (digitised by the North Dakota Constitution project, ndconst.org)
sources.title: Thomas M. Cooley, A Treatise on the Law of Torts, or the Wrongs Which Arise Independent of Contract, 2nd edition
sources.quote: The right to one's person may be said to be a right of complete immunity : to be let alone.
sources.note: Scanned PDF of the 2nd edition (Chicago: Callaghan & Co., 1888), p. 29, section 'Personal Immunity'. The OCR text layer has a space before the colon; quote kept as it appears in the text layer. The same PDF reprints the preface to the first edition, signed 'UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN, ANN ARBOR, December, 1878.' The first edition (1879) is catalogued by HathiTrust (Record 010461084, University of Michigan copy, publish date 1879) but HathiTrust blocked scripted reading, so the 1879 page could not be quoted.

sources.institution: Harvard Law Review (transcript published by the Louis D. Brandeis School of Law Library, University of Louisville)
sources.title: Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis, 'The Right to Privacy', 4 Harvard Law Review 193, footnote 10
sources.quote: 10. Cooley on Torts , 2d ed., p. 29.
sources.note: Warren and Brandeis's own citation for 'what Judge Cooley calls the right "to be let alone"' — the second edition, page 29.

events.locationNote: Cooley taught at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, where the preface is signed; the publisher was in Chicago. Coordinates: the Law Quadrangle area, Ann Arbor.

events.title: Kodak's box camera puts photography in everyone's hands
events.place: Eastman's works, State Street, Rochester, New York
events.summary: George Eastman introduced the Kodak camera in 1888: a hand-held box loaded with film for 100 exposures, sold for $25. The owner sent the whole camera back to Rochester, where for $10 the film was developed, prints made and the camera reloaded. Eastman coined the slogan “You press the button, we do the rest”, and the word “Kodak” was registered as a trademark the same year.
events.significance: Cheap, candid, hand-held photography turned anyone into a potential recorder of anyone else — the technological shock that Warren and Brandeis named two years later.

sources.institution: Kodak (Eastman Kodak Company)
sources.title: George Eastman – history
sources.quote: With the KODAK Camera in 1888, Eastman put down the foundation for making photography available to everyone. Pre-loaded with enough film for 100 exposures, the camera could be easily carried and handheld during operation. It was priced at $25. After exposure, the whole camera was returned to Rochester. There the film was developed, prints were made and new film was inserted -- all for $10.
sources.note: Company page, used only for what the company itself did; date is the access date (page undated).

sources.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History (Internet Archive snapshot)
sources.title: Kodak and the Rise of Amateur Photography
sources.quote: By far the most significant event in the history of amateur photography was the introduction of the Kodak #1 camera in 1888.
sources.note: The live metmuseum.org page returned HTTP 429 to scripts; read via the Wayback Machine. The same essay says Eastman 'coined the memorable slogan: “You press the button, we do the rest.”' Essay first published October 2004 (Heilbrunn Timeline).

events.locationNote: Kodak's offices and works were on State Street, Rochester (later Kodak Tower, 343 State St.); coordinates approximate.

events.title: Punch cards count the 1890 US census
events.place: U.S. Census Office, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: After winning an 1888 Census Office competition — his system transcribed test data from St. Louis in 72.5 hours and sorted it in 5.5 hours, against 144.5 and 100.5 hours for transcription by the two rivals — Herman Hollerith — whose tabulating machine was patented on 8 January 1889 — supplied electro-mechanical tabulators for the 1890 census. Clerks punched each person's answers into cards that the machine read electrically; census clerks tabulated data for nearly 63 million people this way. Hollerith founded the Tabulating Machine Company in 1896; after a 1911 merger it was renamed International Business Machines (IBM) in 1924.
events.significance: The census became the first mass machine-readable record of individuals — the technical root of every later databank and data-protection fight.

sources.institution: U.S. Census Bureau
sources.title: History and the Census: Herman Hollerith and Mechanical Tabulation
sources.quote: On January 8, 1889, Herman Hollerith received a patent for an electro-mechanical tabulating machine. The U.S. Census Bureau used these "Hollerith Machines" to capture and tabulate data from the 1890 Census.
sources.note: Same page: 'Census clerks tabulated data for nearly 63 million people using Hollerith's tabulators in 1890.' and 'In 1896, Hollerith established The Tabulating Machine Company in Washington, DC. In 1911, Hollerith's company and three others joined to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company in Endicott, NY. They renamed the company International Business Machines (IBM) in 1924.'

sources.institution: U.S. Census Bureau
sources.title: The Hollerith Machine
sources.quote: The first two contestants captured the data in 144.5 hours and 100.5 hours. The third contestant, a former Census Bureau employee named Herman Hollerith, completed the data capture process in 72.5 hours.
sources.note: Undated page; date is the access date. Same page: 'Hollerith astounded Census Bureau officials by completing the task in just 5.5 hours!'

events.locationNote: The temporary Census Office (Department of the Interior) in Washington; exact 1890 building not established, coordinates are central Washington.

events.title: Warren and Brandeis argue for a legal “right to privacy”
events.place: Harvard Law Review, Harvard Law School, Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: Samuel D. Warren, a Boston paper manufacturer who had recently left the law, and his former law partner Louis D. Brandeis published “The Right to Privacy” in the Harvard Law Review, vol. IV, no. 5, dated 15 December 1890 (4 Harv. L. Rev. 193). Citing “what Judge Cooley calls the right ‘to be let alone’”, they warned that “instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise have invaded the sacred precincts of private and domestic life”. They argued that the common law already secured each person's right to decide “to what extent his thoughts, sentiments, and emotions shall be communicated to others”.
events.significance: It reframed privacy from walls and property to a person's control over what is communicated about them — the seed of every later consent regime.

sources.institution: Harvard Law Review (transcript published by the Louis D. Brandeis School of Law Library, University of Louisville)
sources.title: Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis, 'The Right to Privacy', 4 Harvard Law Review 193
sources.quote: Instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise have invaded the sacred precincts of private and domestic life; and numerous mechanical devices threaten to make good the prediction that "what is whispered in the closet shall be proclaimed from the house-tops."
sources.note: Same text: 'The common law secures to each individual the right of determining, ordinarily, to what extent his thoughts, sentiments, and emotions shall be communicated to others.' The page is headed 'Originally published in 4 Harvard Law Review 193 (1890)'.

sources.institution: Robert D. Farber University Archives & Special Collections, Brandeis University Library
sources.title: “The Right to Privacy” by Louis D. Brandeis and Samuel D. Warren, Jr. (LDB-100 exhibit; transcript of page 1)
sources.quote: HARVARD LAW REVIEW VOL. IV. DECEMBER 15, 1890. No. 5.
sources.note: Archive catalogue entry gives DATE 12/15/1890 and LOCATION Cambridge, MA (Louis Dembitz Brandeis Collection, Box 67, II.I.a.4).

sources.institution: California Law Review (Berkeley Law Library, via Internet Archive)
sources.title: William L. Prosser, 'Privacy', 48 California Law Review 383
sources.quote: her husband was a wealthy young paper manufacturer, who only the year before had given up the practice of law to devote himself to an inherited business.
sources.note: Prosser, p. 383, on Warren; the next paragraph: 'Mr. Warren turned to his recent law partner, Louis D. Brandeis'.

events.locationNote: Place of publication: the Harvard Law Review at Harvard Law School, Cambridge (the authors practised law in Boston).

events.title: New York's top court finds no right of privacy in Abigail Roberson's case
events.place: New York Court of Appeals, Court of Appeals Hall, Albany, New York
events.summary: The Franklin Mills Company had printed and circulated about 25,000 lithographs of teenager Abigail Roberson's likeness, captioned “Flour of the Family”, without her knowledge or consent. On 27 June 1902 the Court of Appeals, in an opinion by Chief Judge Alton B. Parker, held that the “so-called ‘right of privacy’” had “not as yet found an abiding place in our jurisprudence”. Parker added that the legislature could forbid using another's picture or name for advertising without consent.
events.significance: The loss showed that courts would not stretch old law to new technology — and pointed privacy toward statutes built on written consent.

sources.institution: Court of Appeals of New York (opinion text reproduced by Hofstra University for educational use)
sources.title: Roberson v. Rochester Folding Box Co., 171 N.Y. 538 (1902)
sources.quote: An examination of the authorities leads us to the conclusion that the so-called 'right of privacy' has not as yet found an abiding place in our jurisprudence
sources.note: Same opinion: 'The legislative body could very well interfere and arbitrarily provide that no one should be permitted for his own selfish purpose to use the picture or the name of another for advertising purposes without his consent.' The 25,000 figure is from the complaint as recited in the opinion: 'had obtained, made, printed, sold, and circulated about 25,000 lithographic prints, photographs, and likenesses of plaintiff'. Excerpted copy (some passages omitted).

sources.institution: Historical Society of the New York Courts
sources.title: Who Owns A Photo of Your Face? The Right to Privacy & The Courts
sources.quote: But the Court of Appeals rejected her plea: there was no inherent right to privacy in the constitution and the court could not bestow it. That was up to the legislature.
sources.note: Event page, date of access; it gives Roberson's age as 17.

events.locationNote: In 1902 the Court of Appeals sat in Court of Appeals Hall, Eagle Street, Albany.

events.title: New York passes the first privacy statute: no use of a name or picture without written consent
events.place: New York State Capitol, Albany, New York
events.summary: In its next session after Roberson, the New York legislature passed chapter 132 of the Laws of 1903, which made it a misdemeanor to use the name, portrait or picture of any living person for advertising or trade without that person's written consent, and gave the person a civil action. The provisions became sections 50 and 51 of New York's Civil Rights Law and are still in force. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld the statute against a due-process challenge in Sperry & Hutchinson Co. v. Rhodes (1 May 1911).
events.significance: The first privacy statute was a consent rule: use of a person's identity required their prior written permission — an ancestor of person-set terms.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports via govinfo.gov)
sources.title: Sperry & Hutchinson Co. v. Rhodes, 220 U.S. 502 (1911)
sources.quote: The suit was based upon Chapter 132 of the New York Statutes of 1903, which makes such use of the name, portrait or picture of any living person a misdemeanor and gives this action.
sources.note: Same report, argument for plaintiff in error: 'The statute in this case was enacted soon after Chief Judge Parker's decision in the Roberson case.' Opinion by Justice Holmes.

sources.institution: New York State Senate, Open Legislation (Internet Archive snapshot)
sources.title: New York Civil Rights Law § 50: Right of privacy
sources.quote: § 50. Right of privacy. A person, firm or corporation that uses for advertising purposes, or for the purposes of trade, the name, portrait, picture, likeness, or voice of any living person without having first obtained the written consent of such person, or if a minor of such minor's parent or guardian, is guilty of a misdemeanor.
sources.note: Current, amended text (the words 'likeness, or voice' were added after 1903). nysenate.gov returned HTTP 403 to scripts, so the Wayback snapshot was read.

sources.institution: Historical Society of the New York Courts
sources.title: Who Owns A Photo of Your Face? The Right to Privacy & The Courts
sources.quote: In 1903, in response, the legislature passed the first state privacy law, which is still on the books.

events.locationNote: Legislature's seat: New York State Capitol, Albany.

events.title: Georgia's Supreme Court recognises a right of privacy
events.place: Supreme Court of Georgia, Georgia State Capitol, Atlanta
events.summary: Paolo Pavesich sued after the New England Life Insurance Company used his photograph, without consent, in an advertisement implying he was a satisfied policyholder. On 3 March 1905 the Supreme Court of Georgia, in an opinion by Justice Cobb, held that “the right of privacy has its foundation in the instincts of nature”, that personal liberty includes the right “to be let alone”, and that publishing a person's picture in an advertisement without consent violates that right. It expressly disapproved the majority reasoning in Roberson.
events.significance: The first high-court recognition of privacy as a common-law right rested it on liberty and consent, and said a waiver for one purpose does not authorise use for all purposes — purpose limitation in embryo.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of Georgia (opinion text via vLex)
sources.title: Pavesich v. New England Life Ins. Co., 122 Ga. 190, 50 S.E. 68 (Ga. 1905)
sources.quote: The right of privacy has its foundation in the instincts of nature.
sources.note: vLex shows the syllabus and opening of the opinion without login. Syllabus point 8: 'A waiver for one purpose, and in favor of one person or ciass [sic], does not authorize an invasion for all purposes, or by all persons and classes.' Point 10 disapproves the Roberson majority. Decision date shown as 'March 3, 1905'.

sources.institution: Smithsonian Magazine / History News Network
sources.title: How the Rise of the Camera Launched a Fight to Protect Gilded Age Americans' Privacy (Sohini Desai)
sources.quote: Soon after, the Supreme Court of Georgia became the first to recognize this category of privacy claim.
sources.note: Secondary source for the 'first' characterisation.

events.locationNote: The Supreme Court of Georgia then sat in the State Capitol, Atlanta.

events.title: Olmstead: wiretaps are not searches — and Brandeis dissents
events.place: Supreme Court of the United States, Old Senate Chamber, U.S. Capitol, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: In Olmstead v. United States (decided 4 June 1928) the Supreme Court held 5–4 that federal officers who secretly tapped the telephone lines of a Prohibition-law conspiracy, without trespassing on the defendants' property, had not violated the Fourth Amendment. Dissenting, Justice Louis Brandeis wrote that the framers “conferred, as against the Government, the right to be let alone — the most comprehensive of rights and the right most valued by civilized men”, and warned that “the progress of science in furnishing the Government with means of espionage is not likely to stop with wire-tapping.”
events.significance: Brandeis carried the 1890 idea into constitutional law and predicted that privacy threats would come from technology that never crosses a doorstep.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, Library of Congress)
sources.title: Olmstead v. United States, 277 U.S. 438 (1928)
sources.quote: They conferred, as against the Government, the right to be let alone-the most comprehensive of rights and the right most valued by civilized men.
sources.note: Brandeis, J., dissenting, 277 U.S. at 478. Same report: 'The progress of science in furnishing the Government with means of espionage is not likely to stop with wire-tapping.' (at 474). Syllabus: 'The tapping connections were made in the basement of a large office building and on public streets, and no trespass was committed upon any property of the defendants.' The 5-4 split is from the report's lineup of four dissents (Holmes, Brandeis, Butler, Stone).

events.locationNote: The Supreme Court sat in the Old Senate Chamber of the Capitol until 1935.

events.title: US census law bars using returns against the people who gave them
events.place: United States Congress, U.S. Capitol, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: Earlier census acts had required that census information “shall be used only for the statistical purposes for which it is supplied” (1909) and that only sworn census employees examine individual reports (the act for the 1920 census). The act providing for the Fifteenth Census, approved 18 June 1929, further protected the information from use “to the detriment of the person or persons to whom such information relates”. The same principle — no publication identifying any individual — was later codified in Title 13 of the U.S. Code (1954).
events.significance: An early statutory purpose-limitation promise: data given for counting may not be turned against the giver — a promise that would be broken within 13 years.

sources.institution: Population and Development Review (Steven Ruggles and Diana L. Magnuson), via PubMed Central
sources.title: “It's None of Their Damn Business”: Privacy and Disclosure Control in the U.S. Census, 1790–2020
sources.quote: A decade later, the Census Bureau further clarified that the 1929 Census Act protected the information collected from being used “to the detriment of the person or persons to whom such information relates”
sources.note: Peer-reviewed, open access: Popul Dev Rev 49(3):651-679, doi:10.1111/padr.12580. Reference list: 'Census Act. 1929. “The Act Providing for the Fifteenth Census and for the Apportionment of Representatives in Congress.” June 18, 1929.' The article adds: 'Virtually the same language appears in Title 13 (1954), which has governed the censuses taken since 1960.' The 1929 statute itself was not read.

events.locationNote: Law made by Congress at the U.S. Capitol.

events.title: Nazi census asks about Jewish grandparents — under a promise of statistical secrecy
events.place: Statistisches Reichsamt (Statistical Office of the Reich), Berlin
events.summary: Germany's census of 17 May 1939 came with a supplementary card for each household asking whether any grandparent was Jewish, where the 16 June 1933 census had asked about religion. Respondents were threatened with heavy penalties for false answers but promised discretion — cards in a sealed envelope — and “a purely statistical evaluation”. Cards recording a Jewish grandparent were nonetheless passed, after statistical processing, to the Reich Office of Genealogy; the surviving cards name about 277,500 people in about 130,000 households with their addresses.
events.significance: A census confidentiality promise was used to extract exactly the data that fed persecution — statistical data and identifying data were never truly separated.

sources.institution: Bundesarchiv (German Federal Archives), Nicolai M. Zimmermann
sources.title: The supplementary cards stating information about origin and educational background of the population census of 17 May 1939
sources.quote: In order to obtain correct details, massive penalties were threatened on the one hand while on the other hand discretion of those counting was officially assured; the counters were to receive the cards in a sealed envelope. They also promised a purely statistical evaluation.
sources.note: Undated archive essay (date = access date). Same essay: 'Provided that one of the household members had answered the question asking for a Jewish grandparent with yes, the supplementary cards were brought – after their regular evaluation by the Statistical Authority of the Reich, the State Statistical Offices and the registry offices of the police – to the Reich Office of Genealogy' and 'approximately 130,000 households ... approximately 277,500 citizens with their full name, date and place of birth, their origin as well as their precise address as per deadline 17 May 1939'.

sources.institution: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia
sources.title: Locating the Victims
sources.quote: Aggregated census data processed by Hollerith machines could provide the Nazi government with information on how many Jews lived in a particular German city, since the census of 1939 included data on “race,” identifying who was a Jew as defined by the Nuremberg Laws.
sources.note: USHMM stresses that location and identification of victims 'did not rely on modern technology, as sometimes claimed in the popular media' — see the myth record.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are central Berlin; the Statistisches Reichsamt's exact building is not verified.

events.title: A model Dutch population register becomes a tool of deportation
events.place: Rijksinspectie van de Bevolkingsregisters (State Inspectorate of Population Registers), The Hague
events.summary: Before the German occupation the Netherlands had completed a comprehensive population registration system, praised by statistics chief H. W. Methorst in 1938 for following each person “from cradle to grave”. By early 1941 his successor as head of the registration office, J. L. Lentz, had adapted it into special registers of Jews and Roma (“Gypsies”), and these registers and the related identity cards played an important role in their apprehension before deportation. Dutch Jews had the highest death rate — 73 percent — of Jews in any occupied western European country; Jewish refugees who had avoided registration died at a lower rate.
events.significance: It showed that an accurate, centralised, linked register is dangerous in itself: the harm came from data built for benign administration, once control over it changed hands.

sources.institution: Social Research (William Seltzer and Margo Anderson), Johns Hopkins University Press
sources.title: The Dark Side of Numbers: The Role of Population Data Systems in Human Rights Abuses
sources.quote: These registration systems and the related identity cards played an important role in the apprehension of Dutch Jews and Gypsies prior to their eventual deportation to the death camps.
sources.note: Social Research 68(2), Summer 2001, pp. 481-513, at 487-488 (JSTOR stable URL https://www.jstor.org/stable/40971467). Read from a copy posted for a University of Washington course (CSDE 502). Same page: 'By early 1941 Methorst's successor as head of the population registration office, J. L. Lentz, had quickly adapted this general "cradle to grave" system to create special registration systems covering the Jewish and Gypsy populations' and 'Dutch Jews had the highest death rate (73 percent) of Jews residing in any occupied western European country'. They explain the refugees' lower death rate by the fact that they 'avoided registration'. Seltzer's fuller treatment (Population and Development Review 24(3), 1998) was not read.

events.locationNote: Lentz headed the Rijksinspectie van de Bevolkingsregisters in The Hague; coordinates are central The Hague (exact building not verified).

events.title: Wartime law lifts census confidentiality; data on Japanese Americans handed over
events.place: U.S. Bureau of the Census / Department of Commerce, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: The Second War Powers Act (March 1942) allowed the Secretary of Commerce to supply census information for the conduct of the war, suspending the confidentiality protection. The Census Bureau provided block-level data locating Japanese Americans in California and six other states, and — as historian Margo Anderson and statistician William Seltzer showed from Commerce Department records in 2007 — complied within seven days with an 4 August 1943 request from Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau for the names and locations of all people of Japanese ancestry in the Washington, D.C., area. Congress restored census confidentiality in 1947.
events.significance: The textbook case of data collected under a confidentiality promise being repurposed against the people who supplied it — the reason purpose limits must bind the data, not just the collector's good intentions.

sources.institution: Scientific American (JR Minkel)
sources.title: Confirmed: The U.S. Census Bureau Gave Up Names of Japanese-Americans in WW II
sources.quote: A new study of U.S. Department of Commerce documents now shows that the Census Bureau complied with an August 4, 1943, request by Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau for the names and locations of all people of Japanese ancestry in the Washington, D.C., area, according to historian Margo Anderson of the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee and statistician William Seltzer of Fordham University in New York City.
sources.note: Same article: 'The Second War Powers Act of 1942 temporarily repealed that protection to assist in the roundup of Japanese-Americans for imprisonment in internment camps in California and six other states during the war.' / 'The newly revealed documents show that census officials released the information just seven days after it was requested.' / 'Lawmakers restored the confidentiality of census data in 1947.' The underlying paper is W. Seltzer and M. Anderson, 'Census Confidentiality under the Second War Powers Act (1942-1947)', Population Association of America annual meeting, New York, 29-31 March 2007 (not read directly).

sources.institution: Population and Development Review (Steven Ruggles and Diana L. Magnuson), via PubMed Central
sources.title: “It's None of Their Damn Business”: Privacy and Disclosure Control in the U.S. Census, 1790–2020
sources.quote: The passage of the Second War Powers Act (1942) stated that the Secretary of Commerce, at the discretion of the President, was permitted to “make such special investigations and reports of census or statistical matters as may be needed in connection with the conduct of the war”
sources.note: Same passage: 'Seltzer and Anderson (2007) documented multiple examples of wartime disclosure of individual-level census responses.' Statute cited as Second War Powers Act 1942, Title XIV, §1402, 56 Stat. 186.

events.locationNote: Census Bureau headquarters in Washington (it moved to Suitland, Maryland, during the war); coordinates are the Commerce Department building, whose chief clerk authorised the releases.

events.title: Universal Declaration makes privacy a human right (Article 12)
events.place: Palais de Chaillot, Paris (UN General Assembly, third session)
events.summary: The UN General Assembly, meeting in Paris, proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948 (resolution 217 A). Article 12 provides that “no one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence” and that everyone has the right to the protection of the law against such interference.
events.significance: Privacy moved from national tort law into the universal vocabulary of human rights, framed as protection against arbitrary interference by others.

sources.institution: United Nations
sources.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
sources.quote: No one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to attacks upon his honour and reputation. Everyone has the right to the protection of the law against such interference or attacks.
sources.note: Same page: 'the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 ( General Assembly resolution 217 A )'.

events.locationNote: The third session of the General Assembly met at the Palais de Chaillot, Paris (venue from general knowledge; the UN page says only 'in Paris').

events.title: European Convention guarantees respect for private and family life (Article 8)
events.place: Palazzo Barberini, Rome
events.summary: Members of the Council of Europe signed the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms in Rome on 4 November 1950. Article 8 gives everyone “the right to respect for his private and family life, his home and his correspondence”, and allows interference by a public authority only when “in accordance with the law” and “necessary in a democratic society” for listed aims.
events.significance: Unlike the UDHR, Article 8 is enforceable by a court; its tests of legality and necessity became the frame for Europe's later data-protection law.

sources.institution: Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights
sources.title: Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (as amended)
sources.quote: Everyone has the right to respect for his private and family life, his home and his correspondence.
sources.note: Article 8(1). Article 8(2): 'There shall be no interference by a public authority with the exercise of this right except such as is in accordance with the law and is necessary in a democratic society in the interests of national security, public safety or the economic well-being of the country ...'. Place and date line in the PDF: 'Rome, 4.XI.1950'. Current consolidated text (as amended by Protocols 11, 14 and 15); Article 8 wording is unchanged in substance. Entry into force (3 September 1953) not verified here: the coe.int treaty office blocked scripted reading.

events.locationNote: Signed at the Palazzo Barberini, Rome (venue from general knowledge; the text gives only 'Rome').

events.title: East Germany creates the Ministry for State Security (Stasi)
events.place: Volkskammer (People's Chamber), East Berlin
events.summary: On 8 February 1950 the GDR's Volkskammer passed, in a rushed procedure, a law turning the Interior Ministry's Main Administration for the Protection of the Economy into the Ministry for State Security; it took effect when President Wilhelm Pieck promulgated it on 18 February. By 31 October 1989 the ministry had 91,015 full-time employees and about 189,000 unofficial informers — one for every 89 citizens. Its surviving records run to more than 111 kilometres of files.
events.significance: The Stasi became the reference case for total surveillance by file and informer — and, after 1990, for a person's right to see what the state had recorded about them.

sources.institution: Bundesarchiv – Stasi-Unterlagen-Archiv (MfS-Lexikon)

events.title: Prosser sorts seventy years of privacy cases into four torts
events.place: University of California School of Law (Boalt Hall), Berkeley, California
events.summary: In “Privacy”, California Law Review vol. 48 no. 3 (August 1960), p. 383, Dean William L. Prosser of the University of California School of Law surveyed the case law since Warren and Brandeis and concluded it was “not one tort, but a complex of four”: intrusion upon seclusion, public disclosure of embarrassing private facts, false-light publicity, and appropriation of name or likeness. The article substantially boosted the influence of Warren and Brandeis's essay: courts cited it far more often after 1960 than before.
events.significance: Prosser's four torts are all after-the-fact remedies for harm — privacy as a lawsuit, not as terms a person sets in advance.

sources.institution: California Law Review (Berkeley Law Library, lawcat.berkeley.edu, via Internet Archive)
sources.title: William L. Prosser, 'Privacy', 48 California Law Review 383
sources.quote: It is not one tort, but a complex of four. The law of privacy comprises four distinct kinds of invasion of four different interests of the plaintiff
sources.note: Same page lists: '1. Intrusion upon the plaintiff's seclusion or solitude, or into his private affairs. 2. Public disclosure of embarrassing private facts about the plaintiff. 3. Publicity which places the plaintiff in a false light in the public eye. 4. Appropriation, for the defendant's advantage, of the plaintiff's name or likeness.' Author footnote: 'Dean, University of California School of Law, Berkeley.' lawcat.berkeley.edu blocked scripts (HTTP 202 challenge); the PDF was read from the Wayback Machine capture of 19 Dec 2024. DOI 10.15779/Z383J3C.

events.title: Vance Packard's The Naked Society takes surveillance to the bestseller list
events.place: David McKay Company, New York City
events.summary: Journalist Vance Packard, author of The Hidden Persuaders, published The Naked Society (New York: David McKay, 1964), a popular exposé whose first part is titled “The Mounting Surveillance”. It opens with a typical family of 1964 watched at every turn — the mother recorded by a closed-circuit camera hidden in a store dressing room. Two years later Congress chose Packard as the first witness in its hearings on a National Data Center.
events.significance: It turned privacy from a lawyers' topic into a mass public concern about files and devices — the political energy behind the first data-protection laws.

events.title: Griswold v. Connecticut finds “zones of privacy” in the Constitution
events.place: Supreme Court of the United States, 1 First Street NE, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: Planned Parenthood League of Connecticut's executive director and its medical director had been convicted for advising married couples on contraception under a state law banning contraceptive use. On 7 June 1965 the Supreme Court struck the law down. Justice Douglas, for the Court, wrote that “specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras” and that “various guarantees create zones of privacy”, which the ban on use by married couples violated.
events.significance: The US Constitution names no right of privacy; Griswold inferred one, anchoring constitutional privacy in personal autonomy rather than in property or place.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, Library of Congress)

sources.quote: specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras, formed by emanations from those guarantees that help give them life and substance.
sources.note: 381 U.S. at 484 (Douglas, J., for the Court). Syllabus: 'Argued March 29-30, 1965.-Decided June 7, 1965.' and 'The Connecticut statute forbidding use of contraceptives violates the right of marital privacy which is within the penumbra of specific guarantees of the Bill of Rights.' The scan's OCR scrambles the next sentence across columns, so it is quoted from the LII copy below.

events.title: Congress puts the proposed National Data Center on trial
events.place: Room 2247, Rayburn House Office Building, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: In April 1965 a Social Science Research Council committee chaired by Yale economist Richard Ruggles urged a federal data bank, and a Bureau of the Budget task force under Carl Kaysen was studying access to government statistics. On 26–28 July 1966 the House Special Subcommittee on Invasion of Privacy, chaired by Rep. Cornelius Gallagher, held hearings on “The Computer and Invasion of Privacy”. Gallagher said the thought of Americans' records “neatly bundled together into one compact package is appalling” and floated a new rule under which “a person may have the right to examine his own file”. The hearings set off a national press backlash against the plan.
events.significance: The databank fight produced the first official call for a person's right to see and correct their own file — the seed of access rights, and of the idea that individuals, not just institutions, should hold the controls.

sources.quote: The presence of these records in Government files is frightening enough, but the thought of them neatly bundled together into one compact package is appalling. We cannot be certain that such dossiers would always be used by benevolent people for benevolent purposes.
sources.note: Gallagher's opening statement, 26 July 1966, which continues: 'Perhaps a new concept in file accessibility will have to be- formulated, under ... which a person may have the right to examine his own file, or at least have the right of appeal, so that he can insure the accuracy and com- pleteness of his dossier.' (OCR hyphens as in the scan.) The hearing record says the subcommittee met 'in room 2247, Rayburn Office Building'; it introduces Richard Ruggles as chairman of the SSRC Committee on the Preservation and Use of Economic Data 'which last year submitted a report urging the establishment of a data bank' and names the Bureau of the Budget task force with 'Carl Kaysen, chairman'. Appendix 1 reprints the SSRC report dated April 1965.

events.title: Alan Westin defines privacy as control over information about oneself
events.place: Atheneum (publisher), New York City
events.summary: Professor Alan F. Westin — in 1966 a staff consultant and writer for the Special Committee on Science and Law of the Association of the Bar of the City of New York — published Privacy and Freedom (New York: Atheneum, 1967). On page 7 he defined privacy as “the claim of individuals, groups, or institutions to determine for themselves when, how, and to what extent information about them is communicated to others”.
events.significance: Westin's definition is the direct intellectual ancestor of person-proffered terms: it locates privacy in the individual's own determination of how their information flows.

events.title: Katz: “the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places”
events.place: Supreme Court of the United States, 1 First Street NE, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: FBI agents had recorded Katz's side of telephone calls transmitting wagering information from Los Angeles to Miami and Boston by attaching an electronic listening device to the outside of the public telephone booth he used; the appeals court found no violation because there was no physical entrance. On 18 December 1967 the Supreme Court held that this was a search: “the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places”, and the “trespass” doctrine of Olmstead was “no longer controlling”. Justice Harlan's concurrence set out a two-part test: an actual expectation of privacy that “society is prepared to recognize as ‘reasonable’”.
events.significance: Katz vindicated Brandeis's 1928 dissent and cut privacy loose from walls — but tied it to 'reasonable expectations', a standard that shrinks as surveillance becomes normal.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, Library of Congress)
sources.title: Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347 (1967)
sources.quote: For the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places.
sources.note: 389 U.S. at 351 (Stewart, J., for the Court). Syllabus: 'Argued October 17, 1967.-Decided December 18, 1967.' and FBI agents 'had attached an electronic listening and recording device to the outside of the telephone booth from which the calls were made'. Harlan, J., concurring, at 361: 'there is a twofold requirement, first that a person have exhibited an actual (subjective) expectation of privacy and, second, that the expectation be one that society is prepared to recognize as "reasonable."' Opinion: 'the "trespass" doctrine there enunciated can no longer be regarded as controlling.' Opinion: the indictment charged him 'with transmitting wagering information by telephone from Los Angeles to Miami and Boston'.

events.locationNote: The Supreme Court Building, Washington.

events.title: Title III sets warrant rules for wiretaps and bugs
events.place: United States Congress, U.S. Capitol, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: Title III of the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 (Public Law 90-351, approved 19 June 1968) banned unauthorised interception of wire and oral communications and let police intercept only with a court order. Congress found that “there has been extensive wiretapping carried on without legal sanctions, and without the consent of any of the parties to the conversation”, and that uniform rules were needed “to protect effectively the privacy of wire and oral communications”.
events.significance: The first comprehensive US surveillance statute made consent of a party, or a judge's order, the gate for interception — a consent-or-warrant structure later extended to electronic communications.

events.title: Germany's Constitutional Court: the state may not catalogue the whole person
events.place: Bundesverfassungsgericht (Federal Constitutional Court), Karlsruhe
events.summary: A Bavarian woman fined 100 marks for refusing to answer a microcensus questionnaire challenged the statistics law. On 16 July 1969 (1 BvL 19/63) the First Senate upheld the survey question on holiday travel, but held that it would violate human dignity for the state to claim the right “to register and catalogue a person compulsorily in their whole personality”, even anonymously in a statistical survey. Each person must retain an “inner space” where, quoting the jurist Wintrich, “one is left in peace”.
events.significance: A direct line from the 'right to be let alone' to European data protection: it limited what the state may compile about a person, the precursor of the 1983 census judgment and informational self-determination.

sources.institution: Bundesverfassungsgericht (text via Deutschsprachiges Fallrecht, University of Bern)
sources.title: BVerfGE 27, 1 – Mikrozensus, Beschluss des Ersten Senats vom 16. Juli 1969, 1 BvL 19/63
sources.quote: Mit der Menschenwürde wäre es nicht zu vereinbaren, wenn der Staat das Recht für sich in Anspruch nehmen könnte, den Menschen zwangsweise in seiner ganzen Persönlichkeit zu registrieren und zu katalogisieren, sei es auch in der Anonymität einer statistischen Erhebung, und ihn damit wie eine Sache zu behandeln, die einer Bestandsaufnahme in jeder Beziehung zugänglich ist.
sources.note: Translation: 'It would be incompatible with human dignity if the state could claim the right to register and catalogue a person compulsorily in their entire personality, even in the anonymity of a statistical survey, and thereby treat them like a thing open to inventory in every respect.' Next paragraph: the individual must keep an 'Innenraum' ... 'in dem man in Ruhe gelassen wird und ein Recht auf Einsamkeit genießt' ('where one is left in peace and enjoys a right to solitude'), quoting Wintrich (1957). Facts: the respondent refused to answer 'alle 60 Fragen' and was fined 'eine Geldbuße von 100 DM'. Tenor: the microcensus provisions 'waren mit dem Grundgesetz vereinbar'. The court's own website does not publish pre-1998 decisions in full.

events.locationNote: The Court moved into its building at Schlossbezirk 3, Karlsruhe, in 1969; coordinates are that building.

myths.claim: Samuel Warren wrote “The Right to Privacy” because Boston newspapers intruded on his daughter's wedding.
myths.correction: The story comes from William Prosser's 1960 article, which said the matter came to a head when the papers 'had a field day on the occasion of the wedding of a daughter'. But Warren had himself married Mabel Bayard only on 25 January 1883, so in 1890 the Warrens had no daughter of marrying age. James Barron (1979) instead pointed to press coverage of a cousin's wedding in 1890; Amy Gajda (2008), after reading about sixty newspaper stories, argues the likelier trigger was years of coverage of Warren's family after he married into a prominent political family.

sources.institution: Michigan State Law Review (Amy Gajda), via BrooklynWorks (Internet Archive snapshot)

sources.note: Mich. St. L. Rev. 2008:35, at 38-39. Same passage: 'Moreover, not only did the Warrens have no daughter of marrying age at the time'; Barron's alternative: 'publicity over the wedding of one of Warren's cousins in 1890'. The introduction dates Warren's own wedding: 'Mr. Samuel D. Warren married Miss Mabel Bayard at the Church of the Ascension in Washington, D.C., just before noon on January 25, 1883.' Barron's article (13 Suffolk U. L. Rev. 875, 1979) was not read directly. BrooklynWorks blocked scripts (403); read via the Wayback Machine.

myths.correction: The article was influential in the long run, but New York's highest court expressly refused to recognise a common-law right of privacy in Roberson (1902), and it took legislation (New York, 1903) and a minority of courts such as Georgia's (1905) to establish it. myths.claim: The US Constitution explicitly guarantees a right to privacy.
myths.correction: The word 'privacy' does not appear in the US Constitution. In Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) the Supreme Court inferred a right of marital privacy from the 'penumbras' of specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights; the Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches of 'persons, houses, papers, and effects', which Olmstead (1928) read literally and Katz (1967) reinterpreted.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, Library of Congress)
sources.title: Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965)
sources.quote: The Connecticut statute forbidding use of contraceptives violates the right of marital privacy which is within the penumbra of specific guarantees of the Bill of Rights.
sources.note: Syllabus. Opinion: 'specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras, formed by emanations from those guarantees that help give them life and substance.' The absence of the word 'privacy' from the constitutional text is general knowledge (not quoted).

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, Library of Congress)
sources.title: Olmstead v. United States, 277 U.S. 438 (1928)
sources.quote: The tapping connections were made in the basement of a large office building and on public streets, and no trespass was committed upon any property of the defendants.
sources.note: Syllabus point 3 refuses to extend the Amendment 'beyond the possible practical meaning' of 'persons, houses, papers, and effects'.

myths.claim: The US Census Bureau only released neighbourhood-level statistics on Japanese Americans in the Second World War, never names.
myths.correction: For decades the Bureau acknowledged releasing block-level data but maintained it never provided individual 'microdata'. Commerce Department records found by Margo Anderson and William Seltzer (2007) show the Bureau supplied the names and locations of people of Japanese ancestry in the Washington, D.C., area to the Treasury (Secret Service) within seven days of an 4 August 1943 request. Former director Kenneth Prewitt called the evidence convincing.

sources.institution: Scientific American (JR Minkel)
sources.title: Confirmed: The U.S. Census Bureau Gave Up Names of Japanese-Americans in WW II
sources.quote: The Bureau previously has acknowledged that it provided neighborhood information on Japanese-Americans for that purpose, but it has maintained that it never provided "microdata," meaning names and specific information about them, to other agencies.
sources.note: Same article quotes Kenneth Prewitt, Census director 1998-2000: 'The [new] evidence is convincing'.

myths.claim: IBM/Hollerith punch-card machines were how the Nazis found and identified the Jews they murdered.
myths.correction: Hollerith (IBM subsidiary) machines did tabulate German census data, including the 1939 census's 'race' data, and were later used in the concentration-camp administration to track prisoners' labour skills. But the US Holocaust Memorial Museum stresses that locating and identifying victims 'did not rely on modern technology'; about 4.5 million of the 6 million Jews killed lived in eastern Europe where such technology was absent, and identification was done by paper records. Registers, identity cards and census returns — not the machines — were the decisive tools (see the Dutch register and the 1939 supplementary cards).

sources.institution: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia
sources.title: Locating the Victims
sources.quote: The location and identification of Nazi victims did not rely on modern technology, as sometimes claimed in the popular media.
sources.note: Same article: 'Hollerith machine technology was introduced at the headquarters of the concentration camp system in 1942 and was used there not to locate and identify people to be killed (this was done by paper record) but as a way of managing and tracking data on living prisoners.' and 'About 75%, or 4.5 million of the 6 million Jews killed in the Holocaust, lived in Poland, the Baltics (Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia), and the Soviet Union'. Edwin Black's IBM and the Holocaust (2001) makes the stronger claim; it was not read for this record.
